1:
The chapter opens on the crown of Josiah's reformation, and the witnesses gather first around the exactness of its timing. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the very form of the Hebrew verb — "and Josiah made a passover" — implies that the feast was held after the renewal of the covenant, and he fixes the date from the parallel: 2 Kings 23:23 sets it in "the eighteenth year of king Josiah," and the keeping of it on the fourteenth day of the first month was in strict accordance with the law, whereas Hezekiah's passover had been irregular in point of time, kept a month late as 2 Chronicles 30:2 records. Keil and Delitzsch read the opening sentence as a superscription over the whole account: Josiah held the passover at the very time appointed in the law, and the verses that follow will unfold first the preparations, then the sacrifices and the meals, and finally the character of the festival.

The reformed John Gill adds the one geographical note that matters — it was kept "in Jerusalem," where alone, by the law of the central sanctuary, it might lawfully be held. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the feast to its full height. Many were the feasts of the Lord, but the passover was the chief: it began them all in the night Israel came out of Egypt and concluded them all in the night Christ was betrayed; and of all the Jewish festivals the ordinance of the Lord's supper most resembles it, so that its due observance is at once an instance and a means of the growing purity of the church and the growing devotion of the believer. Yet Henry will not gild the people's spirit. In Hezekiah's passover the great zeal and devout affection of the people were everywhere visible; here little of that appears — it was more in compliance with the king than from any inclination of their own that they kept it, taking some pride in the form of godliness but little pleasure in its power. What redeemed the day was that the magistrates and ministers did their part, the king quickening the priests and Levites and furnishing the sacrifices himself.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke frames the chapter whole: Josiah celebrates his passover, regulates the courses of the priests, assigns the people and the Levites their portions, and so completes the greatest passover kept since the days of Solomon. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the place, Ellicott and Keil the strict legal timing that set it above Hezekiah's, Clarke its unrivalled scale, and Henry both its exalted meaning and the sober truth that a feast may be kept with outward exactness by hearts not fully in it.
2:
With the feast fixed, the king turns to the men who must carry it, and the witnesses read his first act as the marshalling of a clergy long grown slack. The reformed John Gill notes simply that Josiah "set the priests in their charges" — placed them in their offices and their proper stations, that each might execute his own part in the service. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the phrase: it is literally "over their wards," the same idiom used of the temple arrangements at 2 Chronicles 8:14, so that the king appointed them to discharge their proper duties in connection with the rite. And "encouraged them," Ellicott adds, means encouraged by exhortation and instruction, of which he finds an earlier instance in Hezekiah's like summons at 2 Chronicles 29:5.

Keil and Delitzsch fill out both halves of the verse. Josiah appointed the priests according to their guards or posts — that is, according to the service incumbent on each division — and "he strengthened them for the service of the house of the LORD," the strengthening consisting in encouraging speech and in teaching them the duties the law laid upon them. The verb, they note, is the same word for making strong that runs through such passages of exhortation as Nehemiah 2:18, where hands are strengthened for a good work; and they set the whole beside Hezekiah's parallel charge at 2 Chronicles 29:5, where another reforming king had first to rouse a negligent priesthood to its office.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they draw the portrait of a reformation that begins not with the people but with their ministers. A passover kept "according to the law" required priests who knew the law and stood ready in their courses; and Josiah, rather than cutting out new work or devising new methods, called the priesthood back to the order already settled for it — over their wards, in their divisions, at their posts. The encouragement is as instructive as the command. The king does not merely charge the priests; he strengthens them, speaking to their duty and heartening them for it, so that the work should go forward not by compulsion alone but by a clergy stirred up and made willing. Gill fixes the stationing, Ellicott the wards and the exhortation, Keil the strengthening word that teaches as it cheers. The great festival, they show, was built first upon the recovery of the priests to their proper service.
3:
The king's word passes from the priests to the Levites, and the witnesses find in it both a teaching office and a puzzling command about the ark. The reformed John Gill describes these Levites as those whose business it was to go through the several tribes instructing the people in the knowledge of God, his word and worship; he records too an ancient manuscript that reads, instead of "that taught," "who prepared for all Israel the holy things." Keil and Delitzsch confirm the teaching role from the law — the Levites taught the people, as at 2 Chronicles 17:8 — and note that the unusual written form of the word for "teachers" is probably only an orthographic slip for the ordinary participle found at Nehemiah 8:7.

The crux is the command, "Put the holy ark in the house which Solomon built; it shall not be a burden upon your shoulders." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supposes the priests had secured the ark when the idolatrous kings threatened to destroy everything that led to the true worship, and that now, all being restored, it is ordered back to its place, referring the reader to the fuller account at 2 Kings 23:1. John Wesley agrees that "the house" means the holy of holies, whence the ark had been removed by some wicked king, possibly Josiah's father Amon; and he joins the clause about the burden to Solomon's building, so that the temple was raised precisely that the ark might have a fixed habitation and need no longer be carried on the shoulders as in the days of the tabernacle.

Charles Ellicott lays out the interpretive options. That the ark had been removed from the inner sanctuary he takes as implied, the removal falling probably under Manasseh or Amon to save the sacred symbol from profanation, or perhaps required by the temple's repair under Josiah. A third reading, that the words mean "let the ark be where it stands; do not give a thought to your ancient function of bearing it about, but set your minds on present duties," he rejects as too artificial. Keil and Delitzsch settle the last clause plainly: the bearing on the shoulder is no longer for them, as it had been in the wilderness before the temple gave the ark its resting-place, a point they tie to Numbers 4:15. So the witnesses converge on the likelier sense — the ark, hidden or displaced in the evil years, is restored to Solomon's house, and the Levites, freed from the old burden, are turned to the present service of God and his people Israel.
4:
The charge grows more particular, and the witnesses attend to the ordered "writing" by which the Levites were to prepare themselves. The reformed John Gill reads the command as a summons to readiness and diligence — that they make themselves fit to do their work in the sanctuary, and perform it according to the law of God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects the English at the outset: the pronoun in "prepare yourselves" should not be italicized, for the Hebrew verb is reflexive, "prepare" or "sanctify yourselves," not the causative the vowel-points might suggest. They were to do so "according to their father-houses," and "in their divisions," the courses laid down at length in the register of 1 Chronicles 23-26.

The heart of the verse, for Ellicott, is the twofold "writing." "According to the writing of David king of Israel, and according to the writing of Solomon his son" points, he says, to the existence of written memorials of the regulations of public worship which David and Solomon had instituted — and he compares the passage where David himself refers to such a document at 1 Chronicles 28:19. He observes even the difference of the two nouns: the "writing of David" is one term found only in the later books, the "writing of Solomon" another, of the same family as the word used of the tables of stone at Exodus 32:16.

Keil and Delitzsch join this verse to the next, reading the whole as an order that the Levites take their stand in the sanctuary "according to the divisions of the fathers'-houses of their brethren the people," so that a division of the Levites should answer to each father's-house of the laity. The witnesses do not divide. Together they show a reformation that improvised nothing: the king does not invent an order for the feast but reaches back to the settled written rule of David and Solomon, and bids the Levites arrange themselves by it. The passover was to be no burst of undisciplined zeal but a service conducted by the book — the ancient courses revived, the father-houses marshalled, each Levite prepared and sanctified and standing where the old writing had appointed him. Gill fixes the diligence, Ellicott the documentary "writings" and the reflexive self-preparation, Keil the pairing of Levite to layman; and the sum of them is a worship recovered by fidelity to what had been written down long before.
5:
The stationing of the Levites is spelled out, and the witnesses read it as an ordering of ministry framed to serve the people. The reformed John Gill marks the place simply — "the holy place" is the court of the priests, where their ministrations were performed. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the arrangement more exactly: the Levites were to stand "according to the sections of the father-houses of your brethren the sons of the people," that is, the laity as opposed to the sons of Levi, and, in fact, a portion of a father-house of the Levites was to answer to every entire father-house of laymen. Their task, he explains, was practical and menial: the Levites were to slay and skin the lambs, hand the blood to the priests, and give the roasted flesh to the people, as the eleventh and twelfth verses will show.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads "stand" in its liturgical sense of "minister," again in the court of the priests, and dwells on the pastoral wisdom of the pairing. The Levites were to arrange themselves according to the several families both of the people — whom the king calls their brethren, Wesley notes, "lest they should despise them, or grudge to serve them" — and of the Levites themselves. For the passover was eaten by families according to their numbers; so when the paschal lambs were brought to be killed, the Levites were to order the matter that the victims might be distributed to the several households, whether Levitical or lay.

The witnesses do not divide, and the emphasis they share is telling. The whole elaborate arrangement exists so that the ordinary Israelite family, come up to Jerusalem, should find its lamb slain and its portion ready. The Levites are set not above the people but among them, a division to each clan, servants of their brethren in the holy things. Wesley's small caution — that the king names them "brethren" lest the ministers disdain the service — catches the spirit of it: this was a ministry of humility, the sanctified tribe stooping to prepare the feast for the unsanctified multitude. Gill fixes the court where they stood, Ellicott the exact correspondence of Levite division to lay father-house and the humble work of slaying and skinning, Wesley the tender reason for the pairing. Between them they show an order devised not for the dignity of the clergy but for the welfare of the worshippers, that none of the families of Israel should be left without a part in the passover of their God.
6:
The command reaches its point in a triple charge — kill the passover, sanctify yourselves, prepare your brethren — and the witnesses trace the careful sequence it lays on the Levites. The reformed John Gill reads it as a direction to slay the lamb in the manner, time, and place, and for the persons, that the law required. Keil and Delitzsch expound the order of the three verbs: the Levites were to kill the passover, then sanctify themselves, then prepare it for their brethren the laymen, doing throughout according to the word of the Lord by the hand of Moses. The sanctification set between the killing and the preparing, they suggest, consisted in the washing the Levites underwent after they had slain the lamb, before they gave its blood to the priest to sprinkle upon the altar — the same procedure seen at Hezekiah's passover in 2 Chronicles 30:16.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the verse the same way. To "sanctify yourselves" was probably to wash the hands before handing the blood of sprinkling to the priests; to "prepare your brethren" was to prepare the passover for the brethren of the laity; and the closing clause, "that they may do according to the word of the LORD," means "so as to do" — the Levites themselves obeying the prescriptions of the Mosaic law even as they served the people.

The witnesses do not divide, and the whole weight of their reading falls on the extraordinary office the Levites here assume. In the older law each man slew his own paschal lamb; but the great numbers of this feast, and the ceremonial unfitness of much of the multitude, threw the slaying upon the Levites, who killed for the people and prepared the meal for them. It is the same accommodation that had first appeared under Hezekiah, when the Levites had charge of the slaying for the unclean; and here it is issued as a settled command, folded within the strict requirement that all be done "according to the word of the LORD by Moses." The reformation bends nothing of the law's substance while it stretches its administration: the Levites sanctify themselves, slay, and serve, that a people not wholly clean might yet keep the feast. Gill fixes the lawful manner, Keil the washing that sanctifies between the killing and the preparing, Ellicott the Mosaic conformity of the whole; and together they show a priesthood and a Levitical order improvising in obedience, that the door of the passover might stand open to all Israel.
7:
The narrative turns from command to cost, and the witnesses reckon up the king's own liberality. The reformed John Gill reads the round number plainly: Josiah gave of the flock lambs and kids, all for the passover offerings, to the number of thirty thousand — enough, he supposes, to serve thirty thousand families — together with three thousand bullocks. Keil and Delitzsch confirm the account and its source: the king gave to the sons of the people small cattle, lambs and young goats, all for the passover-offerings, for all that were present, thirty thousand head, and three thousand bullocks, and these were "of the king's substance," his own possession, as his revenues are noted at 2 Chronicles 31:3 and 2 Chronicles 32:29. "All that were present," they add, means the whole people who had come up to the feast from Jerusalem and the rest of Judah without bringing lambs of their own.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott refines the terms. Josiah "gave," he says, in the sense of presenting a heave-offering, the same word used of the princes' gifts at Hezekiah's passover in 2 Chronicles 30:24; the "flock" is literally small cattle, to wit lambs and sons of goats; the thirty thousand small cattle were all for the passover offerings, while the three thousand bullocks were for the peace-offerings and the sacrificial feasting that would run through the following days, as the thirteenth verse will describe.

The witnesses do not divide, and the point they press is the sheer scale of the royal charity. The ceremonial services were costly, and it was in part their expense that had let them fall into neglect; the ordinary Israelite, come up to the feast, might well arrive with no lamb to offer. Rather than let the work of God stand still for want of provision, Josiah furnished the whole congregation at his own proper cost — thirty thousand victims for the passover meal, three thousand oxen for the feasting — a bounty drawn from his own estate. Where God had sown plentifully upon the king, the king sowed plentifully upon the people. Gill fixes the numbers and the families they served, Keil the king's substance and the unprovided multitude, Ellicott the heave-offering and the distinction between the passover lambs and the bullocks of the seven days' feast. Together they show a monarch who would not have the poorest worshipper turned away for lack of a sacrifice, and who made the greatest passover in memory possible by emptying his own hand into it.
8:
The king's gift is matched by his princes', and the witnesses attend both to who these givers were and to the sums they gave. A genuine difference opens at once over the phrase "his princes." The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley take them for ecclesiastical princes — the chief of the priests and Levites, whose names follow — Wesley noting that they gave for the use of any of the families as need should be, since the thirty thousand the king had given were thought insufficient for all. Keil and Delitzsch, by contrast, distinguish sharply: "his princes" are the king's princes, the princes of the kingdom, who presented a free-will offering to the people, priests, and Levites; and these are to be kept apart from the prefects of the house of God and the chiefs of the Levites named afterward in the verse.

On the temple rulers themselves the witnesses agree. Keil and Delitzsch identify the three "rulers of the house of God" — Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel — as the high priest Hilkiah of 2 Chronicles 34:9, with Zechariah perhaps his deputy, the "second priest." Charles Ellicott reads the offering as a heave-offering "for a free-will offering," the number of the princes' own gifts left unspecified, so that he suspects some words may have fallen out of the text; and he notes that Hilkiah is introduced quite abruptly. He too names Hilkiah the high priest, Zechariah probably his deputy or "second priest," and Jehiel perhaps the head of the surviving line of Ithamar, still traceable after the return at Ezra 8:2. These "rulers of the house of God" gave to the priests for the passover offerings two thousand and six hundred small cattle and three hundred oxen.

So the witnesses divide mildly over the identity of the first givers — whether the great lay lords of the realm or the chief ecclesiastics — but they unite in the picture of a graded generosity that answered the king's. Josiah had provided for the mass of the people; the princes now provided for the priests, and, as Gill observes, for poorer priests and Levites whom the king's bounty had not reached. The liberality flowed downward and outward, throne and nobles and temple-rulers together stocking the courts with victims, so that no rank of worshipper should want a sacrifice. Gill and Wesley make the princes ecclesiastical, Keil the princes of the kingdom, Ellicott the temple-rulers who headed the several priestly houses; and between them they show a reformation carried not by the king alone but by a whole ruling order emptying its wealth into the feast.
9:
The roll of givers is completed by the chiefs of the Levites, and the witnesses, brief here, mark both the names and the ascending scale of the bounty. The reformed John Gill passes over the list quickly with a cross-reference. Keil and Delitzsch record the six named leaders — Conaniah and Shemaiah and Nethaneel his brethren, and Hashabiah and Jeiel and Jozabad, chief of the Levites — who gave unto the Levites for passover offerings five thousand small cattle and five hundred oxen, and then carry the narrative forward: with these gifts the service was prepared, the priests standing in their place and the Levites in their courses, according to the king's commandment.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the one observation that lifts the bare list into significance. Three of these names — Conaniah, Shemaiah, and Jozabad — had occurred already among the principal Levites under Hezekiah at 2 Chronicles 31:12-15; and he suggests they may be the names of leading houses rather than of single persons, hereditary designations recurring across the generations. If so, the same Levitical families that had served the earlier reforming king are found serving this one, a quiet continuity binding Hezekiah's passover to Josiah's across the long apostasy of the years between.

The witnesses do not divide, and the arithmetic they preserve tells its own story. The gifts rise as they descend the ranks: the king's princes an unnumbered offering, the rulers of the house of God two thousand six hundred small cattle and three hundred oxen for the priests, and now the chiefs of the Levites five thousand small cattle and five hundred oxen for the Levites — the largest single donation recorded, given by Levites to Levites. Where the king had furnished the mass of the people and the temple-rulers the priests, the Levitical chiefs furnished their own brethren, so that every order in the sanctuary was provided for out of the abundance of its own leaders. It is generosity that mirrors itself down the whole hierarchy of the temple, each rank caring for the rank nearest it, and the least of the ministers left as well provided as the greatest. Where a slack and impoverished worship had once let the feast fall into neglect for very want of victims, here the abundance runs over, so that the passover could be kept without stint. Gill points to the list, Keil to the sums and the readiness of the service that followed, Ellicott to the old family names that reach back to Hezekiah's day; and together they show a passover stocked to overflowing by a liberality that ran from the throne to the least of the singing Levites.
10:
With the gifts gathered, the narrative marks the moment everything stood ready, and the witnesses read the short verse as the hinge between preparation and performance. The reformed John Gill takes "so the service was prepared" to mean that everything had been got ready, both for the passover itself and for the feast of unleavened bread that followed, and for all sorts of people, rich and poor alike — none, in a feast the king had stocked so lavishly, left without a part. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it as a summary: the preparations, described in the foregoing verses and to be gathered up again at the sixteenth, were now complete; and "the priests stood in their place" means, more exactly, on their appointed stand, the same posture noted at Hezekiah's passover in 2 Chronicles 30:16.

Keil and Delitzsch expound the same verse as the point at which the arrangements pass into action. The preparation for the festival, set out in the appointment of the priests and Levites and the procuring of the beasts, was now carried through; the priests stood at their posts and the Levites according to their courses, all "according to the king's commandment" — the very order Josiah had laid down when he stationed them in their charges and bade them arrange themselves after the writing of David and Solomon. The service, in other words, unfolded exactly along the lines the king had drawn.

The witnesses do not divide, and the quiet importance of the notice repays a moment's weight. Everything to this point has been command, provision, and arrangement; here, in a single clause, the whole apparatus is declared ready, and the priests and Levites take their appointed stations. The word the writer chooses — the service was "prepared," made firm and established — is the keynote of the chapter, sounded again at the sixteenth verse when all the service of the Lord is said to be prepared the same day. And the thing that holds it together is named twice over: it was done "according to the king's commandment." A reformation that began in the king's exhortation now stands visible in a temple fully manned, each minister at his post, the sacrifices ready, the people provided for. Gill fixes the completeness for rich and poor, Ellicott the priests upon their stand and the summarizing force of the phrase, Keil the passing of preparation into the ordered act. Together they set the stage on which the slaying, the sprinkling, and the feasting of the following verses will proceed.
11:
The sacrifice begins, and the witnesses divide, mildly, over whose hands slew the lamb before agreeing on the ministry of the blood. The reformed John Gill takes it that the lambs were killed by the Levites, following the arrangement laid down earlier. Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way: the Levites slew the passover — the lambs and young goats presented for the meal — and the priests sprinkled the blood of the paschal victims from their hand, that is, the blood the Levites gave them, while the Levites flayed the carcasses, exactly as at Hezekiah's passover in 2 Chronicles 30:17. Charles Ellicott confirms the point and sharpens it: "from their hand" means the hand of the Levites, who caught the blood as they slaughtered the victims and passed it to the priests; and he observes that what had been the exception under Hezekiah — the Levites slaying for the unclean — "has become the rule here."

Against this the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enters a different reading of the slaying. The people themselves, he holds, might slay their own paschal lambs, and then present the blood to the priests, who sprinkled it before the altar; the Levites, on his view, flayed the victims and made them ready for dressing. So a real difference runs beneath the surface: was the lamb slain by the Levites on the people's behalf, as the grammatical witnesses hold, or by the offerers themselves, as Clarke supposes, the Levites' part being only to flay and prepare?

Yet the disagreement is narrow, and on the shape of the rite the witnesses are one. Whoever wielded the knife, the blood was the priests' charge and the priests' alone — dashed against the altar from the hands of the Levites who brought it — and the flaying and dressing fell to the Levites. The grammatical-historical reading fits the emphasis of the whole chapter, that a multitude not wholly clean threw much of the labour of the feast upon the sanctified tribe; Clarke's preserves the older individual duty of the worshipper. What none disputes is the ordered division of the work: slaying, the catching and handing of the blood, the sprinkling upon the altar, the flaying — each act in its place, the priests at the altar and the Levites at the victims, so that the paschal blood, the very heart of the ordinance, should be applied by the appointed hands and in the appointed way.
12:
The verse turns to the portions set aside for the altar, and the witnesses differ over just what "the burnt offerings" here removed were. The reformed John Gill offers both possibilities: either the priests separated out such of the lambs and kids as were designed for burnt offerings for the people, or they removed from the victims the parts that were to be burnt — the fat of the inwards, the kidneys, the caul upon the liver. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley leans to the first: some of the lesser cattle, he thinks, were set apart to be offered as burnt offerings, since even these might be so offered by the law of Leviticus 1:10, and they were put aside lest they be confounded with the paschal lambs meant for another use.

The grammatical-historical witnesses take the other view. Keil and Delitzsch understand "the burnt offerings" as the pieces of the paschal lamb that were to be burnt upon the altar — the same portions separated from sheep and goats when they were brought as thank-offerings, as prescribed at Leviticus 3:9 — laid and consumed upon the flesh of the evening burnt-offering. Charles Ellicott agrees: they cut off those parts of the victims which had to be consumed on the altar of burnt offering, and these are naturally called "the burnt offering" although no special burnt offering was appointed for the passover evening. After separating the proper pieces, he explains, the Levites gave them to the sections of the fathers'-houses of the people, to be presented in turn to the priests for burning; the appeal "as it is written in the book of Moses" refers to the rule that "all the fat is the LORD's" at Leviticus 3:16; and "so did they with the oxen," whose proper portions were likewise reserved for the brazen altar, the rest furnishing food for the sacrificial festivities.

The witnesses do not divide over the substance — that certain parts were set apart to be burnt to God and the rest given to the people — but genuinely over the reference of the phrase: whether whole animals designated for burnt-offerings (Gill's first option, Wesley), or the fat pieces removed from the paschal victims themselves (Keil, Ellicott, and Gill's second option). Either way the care is the same, that what belonged to the altar be scrupulously distinguished from what belonged to the table, and that the passover be kept, in its every portion, "as it is written in the book of Moses." Gill holds both readings open, Wesley the setting-apart of whole victims, Keil and Ellicott the removal of the fat to be burnt upon the evening offering; and the sum is a rite conducted with an exactness that measured out even the pieces of a lamb by the written law.
13:
The cooking of the sacrifices draws the witnesses to a nice distinction the law had drawn between the paschal lamb and the other offerings. The reformed John Gill notes only that they roasted the passover with fire "according to the ordinance," the ordinance of the Lord by Moses. Keil and Delitzsch expound the double treatment: the flesh of the paschal lamb was roasted with fire, as the law of Exodus 12:9 required, while "the sanctified" — their name for the slaughtered oxen, as at 2 Chronicles 29:33 — were sodden in pots, caldrons, and pans, and brought speedily to the sons of the people, the laymen. Against Bertheau they resist the inference that the oxen were therefore consumed as thank-offerings on the same day; the text, they urge, does not say so.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the verse the same way and dwells on its vividness. The paschal victims were cooked in the fire, according to the ordinance of Exodus 12:8; the consecrated things — the oxen — were boiled or fried in the pots and caldrons and pans, and handed with all due haste by the Levites to the laity. The author, he observes, is telling us not only what was done on the passover evening but through the seven following days of the feast of unleavened bread: on the passover proper only the lambs and kids were eaten, while the oxen were slain as peace-offerings during the subsequent festivities and furnished forth the sacrificial meals, as the law of Deuteronomy 16:1-8 allowed. And the clause "divided them speedily among all the people" he reads as a little touch of realism — the meat brought quickly so that it should not grow cold, the phrase recalling the haste of Genesis 41:14. It calls up the whole busy scene, he says: the groups of people scattered here and there about the sacred court, and the Levites hurrying to them with their portions of the savoury meat.

The witnesses do not divide. Together they show a rite conducted with both exactness and warmth — the lamb roasted whole in the fire as Moses had appointed, never sodden; the peace-offerings boiled and carried steaming through the courts; the distinction of the two carefully kept, and yet the whole scene alive with the movement of a great crowd being fed. Gill fixes the ordinance, Keil the boiling of the sanctified oxen and his caution against Bertheau, Ellicott the seven-days' scope and the vivid haste of the serving. The passover kept "according to the law" was not a cold formality but a thronged and hurried feast, the sanctified tribe running with the meat that the people might eat.
14:
When the people had been served, the ministers made ready for themselves, and the witnesses find in this last-served order a quiet lesson in ministry. The reformed John Gill notes that afterward they prepared for themselves and for the priests the passover lambs and such parts of the peace offerings as belonged to them. Keil and Delitzsch explain why the Levites had to do it: the priests, the sons of Aaron, were busied with the offering of the fat portions upon the altar until night, and so could not prepare their own meal; therefore the Levites, having finished serving the laity, prepared it both for themselves and for the priests. They pause over the terms for the burnt pieces, the "whole burnt" and the "fat," weighing why only the fat of the oxen and not that of the lambs should bear the one name, and confessing the need to read the words with more than ordinary care, since in the law all the fat of every thank-offering is alike so called.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it in the same key. After serving the laity with their passover, the Levites made ready the Passover for themselves and the priests — the very phrase, he notes, that meets us in the Gospel account of preparing the passover at Luke 22:8. The reason follows: the priests were occupied in offering the burnt offering and the pieces of fat until night, the second phrase defining the first, so that the sons of Aaron, held at the altar by the endless sacrifices of so vast a feast, had no leisure to dress their own supper, and the Levites did it for them.

The witnesses do not divide, and the picture they draw is of a ministry that served itself last. All day the priests stood at the altar burning the fat until nightfall; the Levites ran with the people's portions; and only when the multitude was fed and the offerings consumed did the ministers sit down to eat, the Levites having prepared the meal for their weary brethren the priests as well as for themselves. It is the reformation's own spirit in miniature — the servants of the house of God bearing the heat of the day, forwarding one another's work, and taking their own refreshment only when the labour was done. Gill fixes the parts that fell to them, Keil the priests kept at the altar till night and the careful sense of the terms, Ellicott the Gospel echo and the reason for the Levites' extra office; and together they leave us a priesthood too busy in the service of others to serve itself until the darkness fell.
15:
The music and the gatekeeping of the feast draw the witnesses to the Davidic order that governed even these. The reformed John Gill sets the scene: the singers, the sons of Asaph, were in their place in the court of the priests, singing and playing upon their instruments while the sacrifices were offered. Keil and Delitzsch gather the whole verse: the sons of Asaph stood in their place according to the commandment of David, and of Asaph, and Heman, and Jeduthun the king's seer, while the porters waited at every gate and might not depart from their service, for their brethren the Levites prepared their portions and brought them to them.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fills in the detail. "In their place" means at their post or station, as the phrase is used at 1 Chronicles 23:28; the sons of Heman and Jeduthun are omitted here for brevity, though they too belonged to the appointed choirs; and the whole ordering rests on the institution of the temple music by David, recorded at 1 Chronicles 25:1-6. The clause "they might not depart," he adds, is better read "they had no need to depart" from their service — the singers and porters did not have to leave their posts to prepare their own passover and the meals that followed, "for their brethren the Levites had prepared for them," and brought it to them at their several stations.

The witnesses do not divide, and two things stand out in their common reading. The first is the reach of the Davidic pattern: not only the slaying and the sprinkling but the very songs and the manning of the gates were done "according to the commandment of David" and his seers, so that the feast was, in its music as in its sacrifice, a service conducted by the ancient rule. The second is the same tender cooperation that ran through the preparation of the priests' meal. The singers could not leave off their psalmody, nor the porters their watch at the gates — the one lest the praise fall silent, the other lest anything unclean break into the assembly — and so their brethren the Levites carried their portions to them where they stood. Gill fixes the singers at their instruments, Keil the porters kept at the gates, Ellicott the Davidic institution and the loving provision that freed each man to keep his post. Together they show a temple in which no voice fell silent and no gate went unwatched, because the Levites served one another that the whole service of God might go on unbroken.
16:
The account pauses to sum itself up, and the witnesses read the verse as the writer's own seal upon the completed service. The reformed John Gill takes it simply: all the service of the Lord was prepared that day, with every sacrifice and for all sorts of persons. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads "the same day" as "at that time," pointing forward to the seventeenth verse, and explains "to offer burnt offerings" as the burning of the fat of the passover victims and of the peace offerings upon the altar; the whole verse, he says, summarises the foregoing account, gathering up again what was first declared at the tenth.

Keil and Delitzsch expound the summarizing force most fully. This statement, like the one at the tenth verse, draws together all that precedes and forms the transition to the closing remarks on the festival: all the service of the Lord was prepared that day, in regard to the keeping of the passover and the offering of the burnt offerings upon the altar, "according to the commandment of king Josiah." And they guard against a false narrowing of the phrase. "The same day," they insist, is not to be confined to the single afternoon and evening of the fourteenth; it embraces the whole time of the festival, just as the word "day" in Genesis 2:4 takes in the seven days of the creation. The one day of the passover and the seven of unleavened bread are gathered into a single span of ordered worship.

The witnesses do not divide, and the note they strike is completeness under command. Twice now the writer has said the service was "prepared" — established, made firm — and each time he has traced it to the king. The passover was no ragged improvisation but a whole liturgy accomplished as one act, the slaying and the sprinkling, the roasting and the boiling, the music and the gatekeeping, all brought to their appointed end "according to the commandment of king Josiah." The verse is a resting-place in the narrative, the point at which the historian steps back to survey a work entirely done before he turns to characterize the feast in the verses that follow. Gill fixes the every-sacrifice fullness, Ellicott the summarizing reference back to the tenth verse and the burning of the fat, Keil the breadth of "the same day" that covers the whole festival and the royal command that shaped it. Together they show a service of God complete in all its parts, and complete because a king had willed and ordered it so.
17:
The verse states the plain fact of the observance — the children of Israel present kept the passover at that time, and the feast of unleavened bread seven days — and the witnesses fasten on the exactness of its timing. The reformed John Gill marks that it was kept "in its proper time, on the fourteenth day of Nisan," the very day the law appointed. Keil and Delitzsch spell out the two-part solemnity: the Israelites who had come kept the passover at that time — that is, as the first verse had said, on the fourteenth day of the first month — and the unleavened bread seven days, from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of the same month. Charles Ellicott fixes the same calendar: the passover on the evening of the fourteenth of Nisan, the feast of Mazzoth from the fifteenth to the twenty-first.

The witnesses do not divide, and the quiet emphasis they share is the strict legality of the date. It is a point the chapter has pressed from its opening, and it repays the pressing, for it is precisely here that Josiah's passover stood apart from Hezekiah's. Hezekiah, finding his priests unsanctified and his people unassembled, had kept the feast a month late by the law's own indulgence for the unclean and the distant; but Josiah kept it in the first month, on the fourteenth day, exactly as Moses had commanded, with no need of the postponement the earlier reformer had been driven to. The "children of Israel that were present" gathers up, as the next verse will make plain, not the men of Judah only but the remnant of the northern tribes who had come south to the feast, so that the observance was as wide in its embrace as it was exact in its date.

Brief as the notice is, it is the verse in which the whole preparation issues at last in the thing prepared. The summons, the councils, the stationing of the priests, the lavish provision, the slaying and the sprinkling and the serving — all of it has been moving toward this: a people gathered in Jerusalem keeping the passover on its lawful day and prolonging their joy through the seven days of unleavened bread. Gill fixes the proper fourteenth of Nisan, Keil the span from the fifteenth to the twenty-first, Ellicott the evening of the passover and the week of Mazzoth that followed. Together they show a feast kept, at last, in the fullness both of its time and of its company — the law's own day honoured to the letter, and Israel and Judah alike keeping it together.
18:
The historian pronounces his great verdict — no passover like it since the days of Samuel — and the witnesses weigh both the comparison and the things that earned it. The reformed John Gill fixes the grounds: it was kept so exactly according to the law, so universally by Israel and Judah together, and with such liberality shown by the king and the chief of the priests and Levites, that none since the prophet's day had equalled it. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the note of liberality. Adam Clarke, citing Calmet, holds that what distinguished this passover from all the former was the great generosity of Josiah, who distributed to his people a greater number of victims than either David or Solomon had done; and John Wesley adds that the whole solemnity was performed exactly according to the law, whereas in Hezekiah's passover there had been several irregularities, and that Josiah furnished the whole congregation with beasts for sacrifice at his own charge, which no king had ever done before him.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the wording and reconcile it with the parallel. Charles Ellicott sets the verse beside 2 Kings 23:22, where the Kings say "from the days of the judges that judged Israel"; the difference is no contradiction, for Samuel was the last and greatest of those judges, as 1 Samuel 7:15 shows. He notes too that the added roll of participants — the priests, the Levites, all Judah and Israel present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem — is not in Kings but is a characteristic addition of the chronicler, and that "Israel that were present" means the remnant who had come from the ruined kingdom of the ten tribes, as at 2 Chronicles 34:33. Keil and Delitzsch read the same way, taking the closing words as a rhetorical enumeration of all who shared the feast, from the king down to the townsfolk of Jerusalem, and pointing to 2 Kings 23:22 for the points that set this passover above the rest.

The witnesses do not divide. Each names a facet of the same pre-eminence: Gill and Wesley the exact legal conformity that Hezekiah's had lacked, Clarke the unrivalled royal liberality, Ellicott and Keil the sweep of the company that kept it and the harmony of the two accounts. What lifted this passover above every other since Samuel was not one thing but the concurrence of all — a feast kept to the letter of Moses, furnished beyond the bounty of David or Solomon, and shared by a whole nation, Judah and the surviving north together, gathered under one reforming king. It is the summit of the chronicler's story of Josiah, and the witnesses let it stand in its full grandeur before the shadow of the next verses falls.
19:
The account of the passover is sealed with its date — "in the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah was this passover kept" — and the two witnesses who remain read the notice as both a chronological anchor and a mark of the reformation's climax. Keil and Delitzsch observe that this closing statement carries the reader back to the same date given at the beginning of the account, binding the whole festival within the eighteenth year; and they treat it as the last word of the passover narrative before the historian turns to the tragic end of the reign. Charles Ellicott sets the year beside its parallel at 2 Kings 23:23, renders "kept" more exactly as "made," and refers the date back to the reckoning at 2 Chronicles 34:8, adding the fitting reflection that "the religious reformation appropriately culminated in a splendid celebration of the Passover."

That single sentence of Ellicott's gathers up the meaning the witnesses find in the verse. The eighteenth year was no ordinary date in Josiah's reign: it was the year in which, as the preceding chapter had told, the king set about repairing the house of the Lord, and in the course of that repair the book of the law was found, read before the king, and made the ground of a solemn covenant renewed by king and people. The passover of this chapter is the crown set upon that year's work. The whole movement of the reformation — the purging of the idols, the mending of the temple, the recovery of the law, the covenant sworn — comes to its head in the keeping of the feast that most bound Israel to its redeeming God, kept now on its lawful day, according to the law just recovered.

The witnesses do not divide, and the placing of the date is itself significant. By fixing the passover in the eighteenth year, the historian ties the greatest of Josiah's religious acts to the very season of his greatest zeal, so that the feast stands not as an isolated splendour but as the fruit and summit of a whole campaign of return. It is the high-water mark of the reign, the point at which the reformation reaches as far as a reformation can — a people gathered, a law honoured, a covenant kept, a passover unequalled since the days of Samuel. Keil fixes the date as the closing frame of the account and the threshold of what follows, Ellicott the parallel in Kings and the culminating grandeur of the celebration. Together they let the chapter rest for a moment upon its height, before the words "after all this" open the descent to Megiddo.
20:
With the words "after all this" the chronicle turns from the summit of the reign to its sudden ruin, and the witnesses feel the whole weight of the fall. The reformed John Gill marks the irony: after Josiah had purified and repaired the temple and set its service in good order, "great prosperity in church and state might have been expected" — and instead comes Megiddo. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the same point into a lesson on providence: when the king and his people hoped that God was reconciled and a lasting happiness founded, their hopes were quickly blasted; "so much are men often mistaken in their judgments about the designs of God's providence."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reckons the interval and the blame. It was thirteen years from the famous passover to the king's death, years passed over in silence because the people, for all this, were not turned from the love of their sins nor God from the fierceness of his anger; and the next news of Josiah is that he is cut off in the midst of his days, before he was full forty. Henry does not spare him: he was much to be blamed for his rashness and presumption in going out to war against the king of Egypt "without cause or call," meddling with strife that belonged not to him. Above all, upon being warned by Necho that God had sent him, Josiah ought to have consulted the oracles of God before engaging; his not doing so was his great fault and of fatal consequence, and in this he walked not in the way of David his father, who would have enquired, "Shall I go up?" Yet Henry balances the blame with mystery: it was not in wrath to Josiah, whose heart was upright, but in wrath to a hypocritical nation unworthy of so good a king, that he was so far infatuated as not to hearken.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott supplies the history. "After all this" answers the like phrase at 2 Chronicles 32:1 and calls attention to the difference between the event and what might have been expected. Necho, king of Egypt, came up to fight "at Charchemish by Euphrates" against the king of Assyria of 2 Kings 23:29 — the last ruler of Nineveh, not Babylon, for the Assyrian empire had not yet fallen — Charchemish being a great Hittite stronghold on the middle Euphrates whose situation suited a march against Nineveh. Josiah went out against him; and since Kings only adds that Necho "slew him at Megiddo," Ellicott judges that the chronicler drew the fuller details of the following verses from another source. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Wesley fix the blasted expectation, Henry the rashness that would not enquire of the Lord, Ellicott the great imperial collision into which the good king flung himself unbidden. Together they set the stage for a death that was at once the king's own fault and the nation's judgment.
21:
The king of Egypt sends to warn Josiah off, and the witnesses probe both the strange wording of the message and the question it raises — in whose name Necho spoke. The reformed John Gill notes only that it was Necho who sent to Josiah. Keil and Delitzsch translate the embassy: "What have I to do with thee, thou king of Judah? Not against thee this day, but against the house of my war" — the family with which I wage war, my hereditary enemy — "and God has said that I must make haste; cease from God who is with me, that he destroy thee not." The idiom "what have I to do with thee," they observe, is the same that meets us at Judges 11:12 and 2 Samuel 16:10.

The great question is the "God" of Necho's mouth. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the opening as the Greek of the Gospels, "what to me and to thee," as at Mark 5:7; over the obscure "house of my war" he prefers the reading behind the old versions and Josephus, "against the Euphrates is my war"; and on the theology he is cautious. The Egyptian kings, like those of Israel and Assyria, consulted their prophets before any expedition — as the Moabite stone has Chemosh command the march against Nebo — and these facts, he says, explain Necho's words "without assuming that Necho had received an oracle from Jehovah, or was referring to the God of Israel." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reaches for the Targum, which turns the speech to idolatry outright: "My idol commanded me to make haste; refrain therefore from me and my idol which is with me, that he betray thee not" — the rabbinical excuse for Josiah, that when he heard Necho name his idol, he would not go back.

So a real difference opens over the source of the warning. Ellicott takes Necho to be speaking of his own gods, on the strength of his own religion; Clarke reports the Jewish tradition that reads it flatly of an idol, and finds in it the rabbis' apology for the king's persistence; Keil lets the word "God" stand as it is, a divine claim laid before Josiah. The witnesses do not settle it here, and they need not, for the next verse will resolve what this one only raises: whatever Necho meant by "God," the sequel would show that the warning was, in the event, from the mouth of the true God. Gill fixes the sender, Keil the hereditary-enemy sense and the Hebrew idiom, Ellicott the Egyptian consulting of oracles and the likelier text, Clarke the Targum's idol and the rabbinic excuse. Between them they leave the reader poised on the very question the tragedy will answer.
22:
Josiah will not be turned, and the witnesses read his refusal both as a textual crux and as the fatal heart of the tragedy. The reformed John Gill takes "would not turn his face from him" to mean that the king would not withdraw his forces and go back. Keil and Delitzsch expound the harder clause: Josiah "disguised himself, that he might fight with him." The word, they note, elsewhere means to disguise by clothing or to disfigure oneself — as Ahab did at 2 Chronicles 18:29 — and here they carry it into the moral sphere: to disfigure oneself is to undertake something that contradicts one's own character, for throughout his reign Josiah had sought to do the will of God, whereas now he went into battle against it. They record that Bertheau would alter the word to "strengthened himself," following the Septuagint, but they keep the received reading.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott flatly rejects their figurative sense. He takes "disguised himself" in its plain meaning, as of Ahab; and he notes that the Septuagint read instead "he strengthened himself," or "persisted," which implies a different Hebrew word — but "it is wholly unlikely," he insists, "that 'disguised himself' is used in the figurative sense of 'departed from his true character,' as Keil and Zockler think." On the next clause, however, Ellicott gives the verse its resolving word. Josiah "hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God"; and this, he says, is decisive: "the warning of Necho was really divine, as the event proved." The valley of Megiddo where the king came to fight was the old valley of the Kishon, where Deborah and Barak had once triumphed over Sisera.

So the witnesses divide over the manner of Josiah's going — a literal disguise like Ahab's (Ellicott), a self-disfiguring that betrayed his own character (Keil, following Zockler), or the Septuagint's "he persisted" (Bertheau) — but they converge on the thing that mattered. Whatever the doubtful verb, the king "hearkened not," and the words he would not hear were, as Ellicott says, from the mouth of God, however little Josiah could have known it from a heathen's lips. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the moral bare: "how can we think to prosper in our ways, if we do not acknowledge God in them?" Gill fixes the refusal to withdraw, Keil the disguise read as a departure from character, Ellicott the literal disguise and the truly divine warning, Wesley the lesson of a king undone by not acknowledging God. Together they show a good man rushing, disguised or determined, upon a word he should have weighed and would not.
23:
The arrows find the king, and the witnesses, few here, catch the pathos of the wound and its dark echoes. The reformed John Gill explains why Josiah, though disguised, was singled out: he plainly appeared to be a general officer, indeed the chief commander, and so the archers aimed at him and pressed him hard. Keil and Delitzsch, whose comment runs on through the death and burial, record the stroke and the king's cry: the archers shot at king Josiah, and the king said to his servants, "Have me away, for I am sore wounded" — the beginning of the swift end that would carry him from that chariot to a grave among his fathers and to the mourning of all Judah.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the scene the deliberate cadence of earlier royal deaths. The shooting of the archers he sets beside the death of Ahab at 2 Chronicles 18:33 and of Saul at 1 Chronicles 10:3 — two kings likewise struck down by the bow. "Have me away," he notes, the Septuagint renders "Take me out," that is, out of the war-chariot; and the very words "for I am sore wounded" are those Ahab had spoken in his dying hour.

The witnesses do not divide, and the echoes they hear give the verse its weight. Josiah had gone to Megiddo disguised, as Ahab once went to Ramoth-gilead disguised; and like Ahab, the disguise availed him nothing, for a chance arrow — no chance in the counsel of God — found the one man it was sent for. Gill's observation only deepens the irony: the very bearing that marked him as the chief commander drew the fatal shaft, so that his greatness betrayed his hiding. The good king and the wicked one are laid side by side in their dying, both pierced by archers, both begging to be carried from the field, both learning that no cloak of disguise can turn an arrow that God has appointed. Gill fixes the reason the king was targeted, Keil the wound and the cry that opened the end, Ellicott the grim kinship with the deaths of Ahab and Saul. Together they show the arrow of Megiddo doing in a moment what all Necho's words had failed to do — stopping the king who would not be stopped, and beginning the sorrow that the following verses will not let the reader forget.
24:
The dying king is borne home, and the witnesses attend to a real divergence between the two accounts of where he died. The reformed John Gill reads the verse plainly: his servants took him out of that chariot, carried him dead to Jerusalem, and buried him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke pauses over "the second chariot," which he thinks may mean no more than that they moved Josiah out of his own chariot into another — either for secrecy, or because his own had been disabled — perhaps the chariot of the officer who attended him to the war.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott faces the harder point. Chronicles says they "brought him to Jerusalem, and he died"; but 2 Kings 23:30 says his servants "made him ride dead from Megiddo." Even if the word there cannot be rendered "dying," Ellicott will not agree with the critic Thenius that the account of Chronicles is simply an arbitrary alteration of the older narrative for the sake of literary effect; on the contrary, "the divergence proves that the chronicler had special sources of information at his command." The "second chariot," he judges, was no doubt a more comfortable one, reserved in case of such an emergency; and the phrase "in one of the sepulchres of his fathers" should drop the "one of," answering to the Kings' "in his own sepulchre," a chamber among the tombs of his immediate ancestors Manasseh and Amon at 2 Kings 21:18.

So the witnesses hold together a scene of tender defeat, differing only over its incidental details — whether the change of chariot was for secrecy or for comfort, whether the king breathed his last on the road or at Megiddo — while Ellicott turns the very difference between the histories into an argument for the chronicler's independent knowledge, against the sceptic who would make it mere invention. Beneath the small textual questions lies the great and bitter fact on which all agree: the reforming king, who had gone out in the pride of his strength against a foe that never sought him, is carried back to his own city in a second chariot, dead or dying, to be laid in the graves of the fathers whose idolatries he had spent his reign undoing. And already the sorrow begins to spread, for "all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah" — the whole people, as the next verse will show, taking up a lamentation that would outlast the generation that raised it. Gill fixes the burial, Clarke the change of chariot, Ellicott the divergence from Kings and the special sources it betrays; together they bring the good king home to his tomb.
25:
The mourning gathers into song, and the witnesses trace both the dirge Jeremiah made and a real question about where it was preserved. The reformed John Gill holds that Jeremiah composed a lamentation for Josiah which is now lost, and he is careful to distinguish it from the canonical book: what stands in the Lamentations, he says, respects Zedekiah and the fall of the city, not Josiah. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same way. Jeremiah wrote a dirge; the singing men and singing women spake of Josiah in the laments they used to sing on the anniversaries of disaster; and they made these an ordinance, a standing custom in Israel. "They are written in the lamentations," he explains, means a Book of Dirges that may have been extant in the chronicler's day, to which the allusions of Jeremiah 22:10 and Zechariah 12:11 point — a collection "quite different from the canonical book of Lamentations, the subject of which is the ruin of Judah and Jerusalem by the Chaldeans."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke widens the setting and reports a rival tradition. The Hebrews, he notes, had poetical compositions for every great and mournful event, funeral elegies commonly made by prophets or inspired men, and Jeremiah's upon this good king is now lost. But the Targum, which Clarke records, identifies the collection with the canonical book: Jeremiah bewailed Josiah with a great lamentation, and all the chiefs and matrons sing these laments concerning him to this day, "and it was a statute in Israel annually to bewail Josiah; behold, these are written in the book of Lamentations, which Baruch wrote down from the mouth of Jeremiah."

So a genuine difference stands. Gill and Ellicott insist that the "lamentations" of this verse are a separate and now-lost book of dirges, and that the canonical Lamentations belongs to a later grief, the Chaldean ruin; the Targum, reported by Clarke, would make them one, ascribing the record to Baruch's pen. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the closing pathos out of the phrase "to this day": in all their succeeding lamentations for public calamities, he says, the people remembered Josiah's death as their first and fatal blow, the stroke that opened the flood-gates to all the miseries that followed. The witnesses do not divide over the fact — a nation's abiding sorrow, a prophet's dirge, a custom of annual mourning — but only over the book that held it. Gill and Ellicott name a lost collection distinct from canonical Lamentations, Clarke the Targum's contrary claim, Wesley the long memory that made this death the fountain of Judah's woes.
26:
The chronicler moves to close the reign with his standing formula, and the witnesses find in its wording a testimony given to no other king. The reformed John Gill reads "his goodness" as summing up two things at once: Josiah's piety toward God and his liberality to the people — the devotion and the open-handedness that the chapter has displayed together. Keil and Delitzsch simply set the closing words in place, "the rest of the acts of Josiah, and his goodness, according to that which was written in the law of the LORD," joining them to the reference that follows.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott draws out what is singular in the phrase. "His goodness," he says, is better rendered "his pious deeds," the same term used of Hezekiah's good works at 2 Chronicles 32:32; but the clause that measures them is unique. That the king's goodness was "according to that which was written in the law of the LORD" is, Ellicott observes, "said of no king besides" — a commendation the chronicler bestows on Josiah alone. And "the book" to which the record is referred answers to the notice at 2 Kings 23:28, there called the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.

The witnesses do not divide, and the weight of the verse lies in that unrepeated praise. Other kings had their acts recorded; other good kings had their goodness noted; but only of Josiah does the historian say that his goodness was measured by, and conformed to, the very law of God — the law that in his eighteenth year had been found in the temple, read in his ears, and made the ground of his covenant. It is the fitting epitaph for the king whose whole reformation had been a return to the written word: his piety and his liberality alike are commended not by the standard of men's esteem but by the standard of Scripture, the rule to which he had bent his kingdom. Gill fixes the double substance of his goodness, piety and liberality; Keil sets the formula in its place; Ellicott marks the phrase that lifts Josiah above every other king, whose goodness the law itself approved. The reign that began in a boy's seeking of God ends with the singular verdict that all his good was according to what God had written — and the reader is pointed, for the rest, to the royal annals in which the fuller record lay.
27:
The chapter ends where the reigns of kings so often end, with the reference of the record to the royal annals — "his deeds, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah" — and here only the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers, drawing out the fullness the bare formula folds away. He reaches, as so often, for the Targum, which expands the phrase "first and last" into a whole survey of the reign: "The former things which he did in his childhood, and the latter things which he did in his youth; and all the judgments which he pronounced from his eighth year, when he came to the kingdom, to his eighteenth, when he was grown up and began to repair the sanctuary of the Lord; and all that he brought of his substance to the hand of judgment, purging both the house of Israel and Judah from all uncleanness; behold, they are written in the book of the Kings of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah."

Clarke lets that paraphrase stand as a fitting summary of the whole story, for it gathers into one sentence the arc the chronicle has traced: the child who came to the throne at eight, the youth who began at sixteen to seek the God of his father David, the king who in his eighteenth year turned to repair the temple and, in the repairing, recovered the law that would remake his kingdom, and the reformer whose zeal reached out to purge not Judah only but the wasted territory of Israel of its idols. "First and last" is the historian's way of claiming the reign entire, from its earliest to its latest act, nothing of a life so full omitted from the heavenly reckoning even where it is passed over in the sacred page.

On the book itself Clarke is plain and sober: "These general histories are lost; but in the books of Kings and Chronicles we have the leading facts." The great royal annals to which the verse points — that fuller "book of the kings of Israel and Judah" — perished long ago; what Providence has preserved for the church is not the whole chronicle but the leading facts, the things needful, gathered into the Scriptures that remain. So the reign of the best of Judah's later kings closes on a double note the witness catches well: a completeness known to God, who has the record of the first things and the last, and a reticence in what men are given to read, who must be content with the leading facts and the singular verdict already pronounced — that all Josiah's goodness was according to what was written in the law of the Lord.
